headline: Flood Recovery and Climate Resilience Dominate Parliament as Child-Safety Bill Passes
summary: Parliament’s first sitting after severe storms and landslides focused on emergency support, damaged transport links and a sharp dispute over long-term climate resilience funding. The Government defended its recovery measures and argued the economy was improving, while opposition parties challenged its climate, cost-of-living and health records. MPs also passed an amendment to the child sex offender register and resumed debate on widening who is formally commemorated on Anzac Day.

topicSummaries.topic: Storm Recovery Prompts Dispute Over $6B Resilience Plan
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: Flooding and landslides have displaced residents, isolated communities and damaged roads, affecting access to housing, schools, healthcare and rural livelihoods.
topicSummaries.content: After severe weather across Northland, Coromandel, the Bay of Plenty and Tairāwhiti, ministers outlined immediate support including $1 million to reimburse marae, $1.2 million for mayoral relief funds, $200,000 for Rural Support Trusts and temporary accommodation such as motorhomes. Transport Minister Chris Bishop said Northland’s state highways had reopened, while major damage remained on routes including State Highway 2 through the Waiōeka Gorge and State Highway 35; full recovery on the latter would take time. Green and Te Pāti Māori MPs pressed for stronger long-term adaptation and direct support, and Labour members criticised the Government for abandoning a proposed $6 billion national resilience plan. Prime Minister Christopher Luxon said that proposal had no money set aside and argued resilience spending was being delivered through existing budgets and programmes. The Government also pointed to a national adaptation framework and flood map under development.

keyExchanges.speaker: Rawiri Waititi (Te Pāti Māori)
keyExchanges.quote: How does he justify his Government’s decision to scrap the $6 billion national resilience plan that was set up after Cyclone Gabrielle, when Aotearoa was experiencing extreme weather events more than ever before?

keyExchanges.speaker: Christopher Luxon (National)
keyExchanges.quote: We have plenty of money available to support the recovery after this event. We are doing that through our roading budgets. We are doing that through our mayoral relief funds and immediate funding. We’re doing it through the Regional Infrastructure Fund and other things that we’ve got going as well.

topicSummaries.topic: Government and Opposition Clash Over Economic Recovery and Household Costs
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: The competing accounts of economic growth, jobs and inflation reflect uncertainty about whether households and businesses will see conditions improve.
topicSummaries.content: The Prime Minister and Finance Minister Nicola Willis pointed to September-quarter GDP growth of 1.1 percent, improving business confidence and other indicators as signs of recovery, while acknowledging volatility in quarterly figures. Labour MPs cited an annual GDP contraction, rising unemployment, company liquidations and hardship withdrawals from KiwiSaver, arguing that households were still under pressure. Luxon attributed the downturn to the previous Government’s record and said growth and jobs were beginning to return; Labour disputed that assessment and highlighted living costs and people leaving for Australia. No new economic measure was announced during the exchange.

keyExchanges.speaker: Chris Hipkins (Labour)
keyExchanges.quote: Does he accept that New Zealanders struggle to believe him when he tells them that the economic recovery has now arrived, given he has been telling them that for the last two years while the economy has shrunk, unemployment has grown, the number of company liquidations has continued to increase, and record numbers of New Zealanders have simply given up and left the country?

keyExchanges.speaker: Christopher Luxon (National)
keyExchanges.quote: There has been a series of leading indicators showing positive economic news that we should all be taking great encouragement from, given the hard work that this Government has undertaken over the last two years to clean up the ungodly mess that he left us.

topicSummaries.topic: Health Data Breach Triggers Review Amid Funding Dispute
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: The incident and the review concern the security of private health records, while the funding dispute raises questions about protection of public health systems.
topicSummaries.content: Health Minister Simeon Brown said Health New Zealand had coordinated an all-of-government response after the private organisation Manage My Health experienced a cyber-security incident, and that the Ministry of Health had begun a review to identify lessons for protecting patient data held by private providers. Labour’s Ayesha Verrall questioned whether Budget 2024 reductions in Health New Zealand’s data and digital funding had led to cancelled cyber-security work. Brown pointed to additional cyber-security funding in Budgets 2024 and 2025 and cited the introduction of 24/7 monitoring; he did not specify which roadmap activities had been cut. The exchange left the funding question contested.

keyExchanges.speaker: Ayesha Verrall (Labour)
keyExchanges.quote: Is it correct that in Budget 2024 his Government cut $236 million from Health New Zealand’s data and digital funding, leading to the cancellation of cyber-security projects?

keyExchanges.speaker: Simeon Brown (National)
keyExchanges.quote: It is correct that we invested more into cyber-security under this Government, with an additional $9 million in Budget 2024 and an additional $10 million in Budget 2025.

topicSummaries.topic: Child-Sex-Offender Register Changes Pass Third Reading
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: The changes expand information and reporting requirements intended to help agencies manage risks to children from registered offenders living in the community.
topicSummaries.content: The House passed the Child Protection (Child Sex Offender Government Agency Registration) Amendment Bill at its third reading, with speakers across parties supporting its child-safety purpose. The bill updates reporting requirements, including requiring notice before a child is due to live at the same address as a registrable offender, and adds seven qualifying offences to the register. Labour and Green MPs supported the bill but raised concerns that applying some new reporting rules to existing registrants could conflict with rights protections and the principle against retrospective penalties. They called for continued scrutiny of the law and broader prevention measures.

keyExchanges.speaker: Mark Mitchell (National)
keyExchanges.quote: The bill adds seven additional qualifying offences to the Act.

keyExchanges.speaker: Duncan Webb (Labour)
keyExchanges.quote: We support this bill, but we do so cautiously.

topicSummaries.topic: Auckland Housing Intensification Plans Remain Unsettled
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: Decisions on where Auckland can add homes will affect housing supply, transport congestion and the cost of finding a place to live.
topicSummaries.content: Housing Minister Chris Bishop said the Government was considering changes to Auckland’s housing-capacity targets and would provide more detail soon. Labour’s Arena Williams questioned whether easing intensification targets would mean fewer homes for first-home buyers and greater reliance on car-dependent development. Bishop said the Government wanted growth around central Auckland, busways and City Rail Link stations, alongside greenfield development where infrastructure costs could be covered. ACT’s Simon Court argued that proposed planning reforms would increase land supply and speed infrastructure delivery; critics in the debate warned that the wider planning and local-government changes could weaken environmental and community safeguards.

keyExchanges.speaker: Arena Williams (Labour)
keyExchanges.quote: Will Aucklanders face more bus congestion and spend more time in traffic under the National Government if density gets dropped in favour of more greenfield development?

keyExchanges.speaker: Chris Bishop (National)
keyExchanges.quote: The choice is not between density and greenfield—or it shouldn’t be. What Auckland and, in fact, New Zealand need is both—or at least we need the choice to be available for landowners and individuals and developers to do what the market demands.

topicSummaries.topic: Anzac Day Bill Would Broaden Recognition of Service
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: The proposed changes would formally include a wider range of people who served New Zealand, including those in conflicts and roles not covered by the current law.
topicSummaries.content: The House resumed the second-reading debate on the Anzac Day Amendment Bill, which would expand statutory commemoration beyond a list of named conflicts to cover service in war or warlike conflicts. MPs said the revised scope would recognise people who served and returned, nurses, merchant navy personnel, people who served alongside the military and those who died in training. Speakers from National, Labour, ACT, New Zealand First and the Greens expressed support, with members crediting cross-party committee work and consultation with veterans’ organisations. The debate was adjourned for resumption at the next sitting; the bill was not passed on this day.

conclusion: The House delivered immediate child-protection legislation and outlined storm relief, but the central political divide remained over whether existing government action is enough to address climate risks, economic strain and pressure on public services.
